style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive prose) + selective amplified study form; narrative register; no divine name inserted
chapterNote: The hinge of the whole book. Mordecai mourns in the open street and sends Esther a summons she cannot dodge: her royal safety is no shelter, deliverance for the Jews is certain from some quarter, but she must choose whether to be part of it — 'and who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' Esther answers with a fast and a resolve that puts her life on the table: 'if I perish, I perish.' Here the hidden queen becomes the deliverer.

1.text: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and ashes, went out into the middle of the city, and cried out with a loud and bitter cry.

2.text: He came only as far as the king's gate, for no one clothed in sackcloth was allowed to enter it.

3.text: And in every province, wherever the king's command and decree reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and wailing; many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
3.notes: The grief is empire-wide and public. This is a people who know how to lament before heaven; though God is unnamed, the sackcloth, fasting, and bitter crying are the posture of a nation throwing itself on the only Help that can reach a sealed, irrevocable decree.

4.text: When Esther's maids and eunuchs came and told her, the queen was seized with anguish. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear in place of his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.

5.text: Then Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to attend her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what this was and why.

6.text: Hathach went out to meet Mordecai in the open square of the city, before the king's gate,

7.text: and Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, and the exact sum of silver Haman had promised to weigh out into the king's treasuries for the destruction of the Jews.

8.text: He also gave him a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for their annihilation, to show Esther and explain to her, charging her to go in to the king to plead for mercy and make appeal before him for her people.

9.text: Hathach came back and reported Mordecai's words to Esther.

10.text: Then Esther spoke to Hathach and sent him back to Mordecai:

11.text: "All the king's servants and the people of the king's provinces know that for any man or woman who goes to the king in the inner court without being summoned, there is one law only: death — unless the king holds out the golden scepter, that they may live. And I have not been called to come to the king these thirty days."
11.amp: there is but one law for him — put to death — except the one to whom the king holds out the golden scepter [sharvit hazzahav], that he may live.
11.notes: This is Esther's real peril, laid out plainly: to approach the king unbidden is death, and the scepter is the sole reprieve, given at the king's whim. Her closing line — 'these thirty days' — hints she cannot count on his affection just now. To go is to gamble her life on favor she cannot presume.

12.text: When they told Mordecai Esther's words,

13.text: Mordecai sent back this answer: "Do not imagine that you alone of all the Jews will escape because you are in the king's house.

14.text: For if you stay silent at a time like this, relief and deliverance will arise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to your royal place for such a time as this?"
14.amp: if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance [revach wehatstsalah — breathing-room and rescue] will rise for the Jews from another place [mimaqom acher], but you and your father's house will perish.
14.notes: The theological heart of Esther. Mordecai is certain deliverance will come — 'from another place' is as close as the book comes to naming God — so the question is not whether the Jews are saved but whether Esther will be found faithful in the hour she was made for. Providence and human responsibility meet in a single sentence: God's purpose stands, and He calls Esther to spend herself for it.

15.text: Esther gave them this answer to take back to Mordecai:

16.text: "Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and fast for me; do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my maids will fast as you do. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law; and if I perish, I perish."
16.notes: Fasting, in Scripture, is turning to God in dependence — though His name is withheld, Esther will not go in her own strength. Her final words are the surrender that makes her a savior of her people: not reckless, but resolved, laying down the very life the crown was meant to protect. 'If I perish, I perish.'

17.text: So Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had commanded him.
